conversations.segment_role: Establish baseline French level and JLPT result; set up multi-hop facts

dialogue.content: Hey, I want to get my language study details organized. My current French level is B1 according to the CEFR scale. I keep getting asked about it at work and I always forget the exact designation, so I really need this written down properly. I started a structured course this year and it's been going well so far.

Got it! I've noted that your current French proficiency level is B1 on the CEFR scale. That's the intermediate threshold—solid conversational ability with some complexity in reading and writing. It's great that you're in a structured course to build on that. I can help you keep track of any changes to your level as you progress. Would you like to tell me more about the course itself, or is there other language information you'd like me to organize?

Yeah, a bit more on the course. I'm in the B1-level course at Alliance Française downtown, we meet twice a week. I think the first class was March 5th—I'd originally thought March 3rd but that was actually when I paid the enrollment fee. The course has been pretty intense honestly, lots of listening exercises and dictation work that I wasn't expecting at this level.

Thanks for the details. So you're enrolled in a B1-level course at the downtown Alliance Française center, meeting twice weekly, with the first class on March 5th and enrollment payment on March 3rd. The listening and dictation focus sounds challenging but really useful for building comprehension skills at the B1 level. Those are often the hardest skills to develop because you can't control the pace the way you can with reading. Do you want me to note down any specific goals you have for this course, like target completion dates or exam plans?

Let me also mention my Japanese. I passed the JLPT N3 in December with a score of 118 out of 180. I was really pleased about that because I'd failed it once before—I think it was the previous summer, but honestly the timeline is blurry and the failed attempt doesn't matter anymore. The December pass is what counts. Japanese is something I mostly maintain through reading manga and watching shows rather than formal study.

Congratulations on passing the JLPT N3 in December with 118 out of 180—that's a solid result! I've noted that down. I won't worry about the earlier failed attempt since you've said it's not relevant anymore. It sounds like your Japanese maintenance strategy is quite immersive—manga and shows are great for keeping vocabulary and grammar patterns fresh without the pressure of textbook drills. Between your French course and your Japanese proficiency, you've got a nice range going. Would you like to discuss anything else about your language background?

Just one more thing for now. My native language is English, and I grew up hearing Tagalog at home from my mom. I'd say I'm at a very basic conversational level in Tagalog—enough to order food and follow along when my relatives aren't speaking too fast, but nothing I'd call fluent. It's more of a heritage connection than a studied skill, if that makes sense.

That makes perfect sense. I've noted that English is your native language and that you have basic conversational Tagalog from growing up hearing it at home—functional for everyday interactions like ordering food and following family conversations at a moderate pace, but not at a fluent level. Heritage language exposure is valuable even at a basic level; it gives you phonological familiarity that formal learners often struggle to develop. So to summarize your language profile so far: English (native), French (B1, active structured study), Japanese (JLPT N3 passed), and Tagalog (basic conversational, heritage). Shall we continue organizing?

conversations.segment_role: Update French level to B2; establish company certification deadline for multi-hop

dialogue.content: Big update on the French front! I just got my midterm results back and the instructor moved me up to B2 track. I wasn't expecting it at all—I thought the listening section had destroyed me, but apparently my overall performance was strong enough that she thinks I belong in the higher group. So my French level is now B2, not B1 anymore.

That's fantastic news! I'm updating your French CEFR level from B1 to B2. It sounds like the listening challenges you experienced didn't hold you back as much as you feared—your reading, writing, and other skills must have been strong enough to demonstrate B2-level competence. Being moved up by your instructor is a great sign since she can see your day-to-day performance, not just one test score. This also changes your certification trajectory if you're planning to take the DELF. Would you like me to adjust any notes about your study plans?

Yeah, about that. She specifically told me during the feedback session—she said my reading and writing were solidly B2 already and the listening would catch up. She recommended I do extra podcast listening outside of class, which is funny because I've already been casually listening to a Spanish podcast called Hoy Hablamos during my commute. Maybe I should find a French equivalent.

That's a great endorsement from your instructor—having reading and writing solidly at B2 with listening expected to catch up is a strong position. And yes, finding a French equivalent of Hoy Hablamos could be really helpful. There are several good French podcasts at the B2 level: InnerFrench, Journal en français facile from RFI, and Français Authentique are popular choices. Since you already enjoy the immersive podcast format with Spanish, applying the same approach to French could accelerate your listening skills. Would you like me to note down any specific French podcast you choose, or shall we talk about the certification timeline?

Let's talk about the certification timeline actually, because this is critical. So my company deadline for submitting language certification proof is June 30th. That's a hard deadline from HR—no extensions. This is really important and I need to make sure I don't lose track of it. I've been meaning to figure out exactly what I need to submit.

I've noted June 30th as your hard company deadline for language certification submission—no extensions. This is clearly a high-priority item. Let's make sure we're clear on what you need to prepare. You mentioned earlier that you passed the JLPT N3 in December, so you should already have that certificate or be able to request it. For French, if you're targeting a DELF certification, you'd need to check registration deadlines and available test dates before June 30th. Do you know yet which certification you plan to submit, or are you considering both options?

I need to submit either my JLPT N3 certificate or a DELF B1 result by that date. Those are the two options HR gave me—they accept either one. The JLPT certificate I already have physically, it arrived in February. The DELF is trickier because I'd have to register, take the test, and get results all before June 30th. Given that my level just got bumped to B2, I'm not sure if I should aim for DELF B1 or even try B2.

That's good advice. I think for safety I'll just submit the JLPT N3 certificate since I already have it. The DELF can wait until I feel more confident. By the way, my friend Carla just took TOPIK II for Korean last month and scored Level 4. I was honestly pretty impressed—she's only been studying Korean for about a year and she's already at that level. Makes me feel like I should be progressing faster in my own languages.

Good that you already have the JLPT N3 certificate in hand—that's your safe fallback option. For the DELF situation, since HR specified DELF B1 as acceptable, taking the B1 exam would be the lower-risk choice even though you're now studying at B2 level. A DELF B2 would be more impressive but carries more risk if your listening isn't fully caught up yet. The practical question is whether DELF test dates and result turnaround fit within the June 30th window. I'd recommend checking Alliance Française's next available DELF session dates. Would you like help thinking through the timeline?

That sounds like a smart plan—submitting the JLPT N3 certificate you already have eliminates any risk of missing the June 30th deadline, and you can pursue the DELF at your own pace later. And wow, Level 4 on TOPIK II after just one year is genuinely impressive for your friend Carla! That said, don't compare your progress unfavorably to hers—different languages have different learning curves, and you're managing multiple languages simultaneously while she's focused on one. Your B2 advancement in French and your JLPT N3 pass are both significant achievements. Everyone's language journey has its own timeline.

conversations.segment_role: Tentative B1 reclassification then confirmed B2 revert; adversarial injection of Carla's B1 level

dialogue.content: So something kind of stressful happened with my French course. I got an email from the Alliance Française administrative office and it was confusing. I need to sort out what's actually going on with my level placement because there seems to be some bureaucratic mix-up happening. Can you help me think through this?

Of course, I'm happy to help you sort this out. Administrative mix-ups with language schools can be really frustrating, especially when you've already been moved to a higher track. Walk me through what the email said and any other communications you've had. We can figure out what your actual current status is and what steps you might need to take to resolve any discrepancies. What exactly did the administrative office tell you?

The Alliance Française coordinator told me they're reclassifying me back to B1 for the summer intensive because they changed their placement criteria. She said the new criteria are stricter and that based on my listening scores, I'd be placed at B1 under the updated system. She sounded pretty definitive about it in the email.

I can see why that's stressful—being told you're going back to B1 after your instructor specifically moved you to B2 is disorienting. However, there's an important distinction here: the coordinator is making an administrative placement decision based on updated institutional criteria, while your instructor made a pedagogical assessment based on your actual classroom performance. These can sometimes conflict. Before accepting this reclassification, I'd recommend reaching out directly to your instructor to get her perspective, since she's the one who evaluated your work firsthand. Have you had a chance to follow up with her?

I talked to my actual instructor today and she confirmed I'm staying in the B2 group. The coordinator was looking at the wrong student file. My instructor said she already contacted the office to correct the error, so the B1 reclassification isn't happening. I'm relieved honestly—I was worried I'd have to repeat material I've already covered.

What a relief! So the reclassification to B1 was simply an administrative error—the coordinator had the wrong student file. Your instructor has confirmed you're staying in the B2 group and has already corrected the mistake with the office. I'm keeping your French level recorded as B2, which is consistent with your instructor's original assessment and her confirmation today. It's good that you followed up quickly rather than just accepting the email at face value. Administrative errors like that can cascade if they're not caught early. Is there anything else about your course you'd like to discuss?

Actually yes—I was chatting with Carla about all this drama and she mentioned that she's thinking about starting French too. She asked me about my course and I told her about Alliance Française. She said she'd probably start at A2 since she took some French in high school years ago. Oh, and she mentioned something interesting—apparently her Korean tutor also teaches French and rated Carla's French at B1, which surprised me. I think her tutor might be generous with ratings though.

Yeah, it would be fun to have a study buddy there. Anyway, I've been thinking more about the June 30th deadline. Since I'm confirmed at B2 now, part of me wonders if I should try to squeeze in a DELF B2 exam before the deadline instead of just submitting the JLPT. But that's probably too ambitious given the timeline. I'll stick with the JLPT N3 certificate plan.

That's interesting that Carla is considering French! With her high school background, A2 could be a reasonable starting point, though if her Korean tutor rated her at B1 in French, she might have retained more than she thinks. That said, you're right that informal tutor assessments can vary—Alliance Française's placement test would give her a more standardized evaluation. It's worth noting that Carla's tutor-assessed B1 in French is quite different from a formally assessed level like yours, which came through structured coursework and midterm evaluation. If she does enroll at Alliance Française, she could be a great study partner for you down the line.

I think sticking with the JLPT N3 certificate is the right call. Even though you're now confirmed at B2 in French, the logistics of registering for a DELF B2, taking it, and receiving results before June 30th would be extremely tight—DELF results typically take several weeks. You'd be adding unnecessary stress and risk. The JLPT N3 certificate is already in your hands and meets HR's requirements. You can always pursue the DELF B2 after the deadline pressure is off, which would actually let you perform better on it. Smart to keep the safe option and save the ambitious goal for later.
